Skin of My Teeth
SKIN uv my TEETH
noun phrase, in ‘by the skin of my teeth’ (only just, narrowly)
The phrase is word for word from the King James Version of Job 19:20: "I am escaped with the skin of my teeth." English keeps it in the idiom by the skin of my teeth, meaning by the narrowest margin. The key word is skin (Oxford English Dictionary).

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To escape by the skin of my teeth is to escape by the smallest possible margin. The words are Job’s. Stripped of his children, his goods and his health, and mocked by his friends, he describes how little is left of him: "My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh, and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth" (Job 19:20). He had come through with almost nothing. The Christian observation: the same chapter does not end in despair. A few verses later Job makes one of the great confessions of the Old Testament: "For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth" (Job 19:25), and "yet in my flesh shall I see God" (Job 19:26). The man who had barely escaped still had the one thing that mattered.

Webster 1828 Definition

Only just, by the narrowest margin; from Job’s complaint, "I am escaped with the skin of my teeth" (Job 19:20), spoken in the chapter where he confesses, "I know that my redeemer liveth" (Job 19:25).

SKIN OF MY TEETH, n. phr. In by the skin of my teeth: barely, with nothing to spare. From Job 19:20 (KJV).

Scripture setting: Job, reduced to almost nothing, who still confesses a living Redeemer (Job 19:25–26).

Key Scripture

Job 19:20 — "My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh, and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth."

Job 19:25 — "For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth:"

Job 19:26 — "And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God:"

Modern Corruption

The idiom keeps Job’s narrow escape and forgets the Redeemer he confessed in the same chapter.

expand to see more

Men use the phrase for a close call: a test passed, a deadline met, a wreck avoided. It has become a light thing. In Job it was not light. He had lost nearly everything, and his friends were accusing him.

The chapter that gives us the phrase also gives one of the clearest hopes of resurrection in the Old Testament (Job 19:25–26). A man may come through with almost nothing and still have everything, if his Redeemer lives.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

skin (OED) → "I am escaped with the skin of my teeth" (Job 19:20, KJV) → idiom by the skin of my teeth.

""We made the last flight out by the skin of our teeth.""

"I am escaped with the skin of my teeth. (Job 19:20)."

"For I know that my redeemer liveth. (Job 19:25)."
